exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Vector From Position Vectors and then Computing its Magnitude

question.text: Let $A(-2,0)$ and $B(3,3).$ Find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation: We have \begin{align*} &\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = -2\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j}, \\ &\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b} = 3\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}. \end{align*} Expressing $\overrightarrow{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain: \begin{align*} \overrightarrow{AB} &= \overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA} \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \\[3pt] &= (3\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) - (-2\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j}) \\[3pt] &= 5\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}. \end{align*} Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get \begin{align*} |\overrightarrow{AB}| &= \sqrt{5^2+3^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{25+9} \\[3pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\sqrt{34}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Points $A$ and $C$ are shown in the picture above. Find $|\overrightarrow{AC}|.$
question.explanation:
From the picture, we obtain $A(0,3)$ and $C(4,0).$ So, we have

\begin{align*} &\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = 0\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}, \\[3pt] &\overrightarrow{OC} = \mathbf{c} = 4\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Expressing $\overrightarrow{AC}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{AC} &= \overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OA}\\[3pt] &= \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a} \\[3pt] &= (4\mathbf{i}) - \left( 3\mathbf{j}\right) \\[3pt] &= 4\mathbf{i} -3 \mathbf{j} \end{align*}

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

\begin{align*} |\overrightarrow{AC}| &= \sqrt{(4)^2+(-3)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{16+9}\\[3pt] &= \sqrt{25}\\[3pt] &=5. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Vector From Position Vectors and then Computing its Magnitude

question.text: Let $A(0,3)$ and $B(4,-1).$ Find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation: We have \begin{align*} &\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = 0\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}, \\ &\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}. \end{align*} Expressing $\overrightarrow{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain: \begin{align*} \overrightarrow{AB} &= \overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA} \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \\[3pt] &= (4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) - (0\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \\[3pt] &= 4\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}. \end{align*} Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get \begin{align*} |\overrightarrow{AB}| &= \sqrt{4^2+(-4)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{16+16} \\[3pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{4\sqrt{2}}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector

question.text: Let $\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}$ and points the same direction.
question.explanation:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction., we need to divide the given vector by its length: \begin{align} \mathbf{u} &= \dfrac{3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}}{|3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}|} \end{align}

First, let's compute the sum:

\begin{align*} 3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s} &= 3 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} (-6)+0 \\ 3+(-6) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

\begin{align*} |3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}| &= \sqrt{(-6)^2+(-3)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{45} \\[3pt] &= 3\sqrt{5}. \end{align*}

Finally, we divide $3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u} &= \dfrac{3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}}{|3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}(3\mathbf{r}+2\mathbf{s}) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{5}} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector

question.text: Let $\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{r}$ and points the same direction.
question.explanation:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction, we need to divide the given vector by its length: \begin{align} \mathbf{u} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\,\mathbf{r}\,|} \end{align}

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

\begin{align*} |\,\mathbf{r}\,| &= \sqrt{(-3)^2+(-6)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{9+36} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{45} \\[3pt] &= 3\sqrt{5}. \end{align*}

Finally, we divide $\mathbf{r}$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{5}} \cdot \mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{5}} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
